slides.headline:
Eight parts of Seoul
the closing-hours law
cannot touch.
slides.subline: It is a legal status, not a reputation. Here is what it does, where it applies, and what it does not promise

slides.label: Seoul neighbourhoods hold the designation. Inside one, the law a district office would use to impose closing hours on restaurants and bars does not apply at all
slides.note: 37 zones nationwide across 14 provinces and metropolitan cities · Sources: Tourism Promotion Act art. 74; Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism designation table, July 2026 · Checked 31 October 2026

slides.title:
A power removed,
not a licence given.
slides.body:
Article 43 of the Food Sanitation Act lets a district office restrict the trading hours and the conduct of food and drink businesses where it judges public order requires it. The limit is set by municipal ordinance, and the Enforcement Decree caps any hours restriction at eight hours a day.

Article 74 of the Tourism Promotion Act then switches that off: inside a designated special tourist zone, Article 43 does not apply. So the zone does not grant anyone the right to trade late. It takes away the instrument the district would otherwise reach for.

items.t: At most ten per cent unrelated land
items.d: Forest, farmland, industrial sites and housing plots with no direct tourism use are capped, and the area cannot be split into separate pieces

items.t: The district applies, the city designates
items.d: A gu office files; the metropolitan or provincial government grants it. The gu must then run a standing promotion plan for the zone
The ministry and the city assess how the plan is being delivered. A zone that stops meeting the bar can have its boundary cut or its status revoked

It is narrow, too — it disables the Food Sanitation Act route only. This post is research, not a personal visit; every rule is from a published source, checked 31 October 2026.

caption:
Eight Seoul neighbourhoods carry a legal status most visitors never hear about, and it quietly explains why the lights stay on.

Article 43 of the Food Sanitation Act lets a district office restrict the trading hours and conduct of food and drink businesses where it judges public order requires it. The limit is set by municipal ordinance and the Enforcement Decree caps it at eight hours a day. Article 74 of the Tourism Promotion Act then removes that power outright: inside a designated special tourist zone, Article 43 does not apply.

Seoul has eight, and the list is a fair map of where the city puts its visitors. Itaewon came first in 1997, then Myeongdong–Namdaemun–Bukchangdong–Dadong–Mugyodong in 2000, Dongdaemun Fashion Town in 2002, Jongno–Cheonggye in 2006, Jamsil in 2012, Gangnam MICE in 2014, Hongdae Culture and Arts in 2021, and the Express Bus Terminal–Sebit zone on the Han River in December 2024. Nationwide there are 37 across 14 provinces and metropolitan cities, on the ministry's July 2026 count.

They are smaller than you would guess. Gangnam MICE is 0.19 km² and Itaewon 0.39 — a few blocks, not a district. To qualify an area needs 500,000 foreign visitors a year in Seoul, 100,000 elsewhere, no more than ten per cent of its land in uses unrelated to tourism, and an unbroken boundary. A gu office applies, the city designates, and the status can be revoked if the area stops meeting the bar.

One honest caveat, because it is the part that misleads people. The exemption removes a power; it creates no obligation. Nothing in it requires a single shop to stay open, so a zone is not a promise that anything is serving at 3am — check the place, not the postcode. It is narrow as well: it disables the Food Sanitation Act route only. Emergency closing orders run on a different law, which is why the 2020–21 curfews reached these zones like everywhere else.

Sources in the last slide. Research, not a visit.
